chapter_title: Documentation, Reporting, and Communication for Site Characterization

sections.title: Geotechnical Reporting and Data Management
sections.summary: Documentation is critical for communicating site characterization results. Four report types: (1) field investigation logs — factual only; (2) geotechnical data report — investigations + factual test results; may be legally binding in bid package; (3) geotechnical design report — includes interpretations, design parameters, and recommendations; not in bid documents; (4) geotechnical baseline report (GBR) — contractually binding baseline for key parameters in design-build and tunneling contracts. Design profiles show measurements with interpretation per stratum. DIGGS standard for data management.
sections.body:
Documentation objectives: Effectively communicate site characterization findings to all relevant parties (designers, constructors, owner representatives, public). Documentation creates a record that may serve legal and contractual purposes. Geotechnical data reports with factual data only may be included in bid documents and become legally binding; geotechnical design reports generally are not included due to professional interpretation content.

Geotechnical data report contents: Introduction; scope of work; site description (location, existing conditions, surface topography); field investigation program (boring/sounding locations with site plan, boring logs, in situ test logs, groundwater monitoring logs); laboratory test reports; appendices with raw data. Factual data only — no interpretations.

Geotechnical design report contents: Introduction; site description; stratigraphy interpretation; design parameters for soil (Section 4.1); design parameters for rock (Section 4.2); groundwater conditions (Section 4.4); recommendations for design (Section 5); recommendations for construction (Section 6); recommendations for inspection, instrumentation, and monitoring. May include geotechnical data report content by reference.

Geotechnical baseline report (GBR): Establishes contractually binding 'baseline' interpretations for parameters with greatest influence on construction risks. Used on design-build, tunneling, and high-risk underground projects. GBR should NOT baseline all parameters — only those that significantly affect construction method, schedule, and cost. Described in ASCE (2007).

Documentation of site characterization activities: Site plan showing boring and sounding locations. Final boring logs with USCS descriptions, SPT data, sample records, and groundwater observations (Figures 13-2, 13-3). CPTU logs (Figure 13-4). Lab test reports: individual reports + summary tables (Figures 13-5 through 13-8). Design profiles: measurements with interpretation trend for each stratum (Figure 13-9). Design cross-sections: interpreted stratigraphy at appropriate scale (Figure 13-10).

Geotechnical data management systems: Electronic databases (DIGGS, AGOL, etc.) increasingly used for multi-project data storage and retrieval. Benefits: search across projects, QA/QC, trend analysis, design-build data sharing. DIGGS (Digital Interchange for Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Data) is the primary industry standard for geotechnical data exchange.
key_points: Data report: factual only; may be legally binding part of bid documents — no interpretations
Design report: includes interpretations and recommendations; not in bid documents
GBR: contractually binding baseline for specific parameters only — used on design-build and tunnel contracts
Design profiles show measurements with interpreted trend per stratum (Figure 13-9)
DIGGS standard for geotechnical data management and exchange
